per_depth.common_affordance: The statement explicitly enumerates the complete set of valid certificates as one-job sequential length or one-appliance total workload, together with a promise that one and only one case applies.
The statement reduces certification to direct additive arithmetic: an isolated JOB has duration p1 + p2, while appliance overload is detected by summing all p1 or all p2 values.
The statement explicitly reduces the supposedly scheduling-based task to an exhaustive decision tree consisting of the per-job inequality p1 + p2 > T and the two aggregate load inequalities.
The explicit promise that every impossible instance has exactly one of two simple certificates: p1+p2>T for some job, or a phase total exceeding T.
the promise that exactly one explicitly characterized local inequality is sufficient, so the answer can be obtained by checking p1+p2>T and the two column sums without scheduling
The relaxed scenarios completely decouple the problem into additive necessary conditions: p1+p2 for an isolated query, sum(p1) for Scenario B, and sum(p2) for Scenario C.

The intrinsic one-dimensional interval-packing fact that pairwise disjoint positive-length intervals contained in a horizon of length T have total length at most T, together with the single-job precedence bound p1_i + p2_i <= T.

The certificate subsystems collapse to one-dimensional interval-capacity inequalities: JOB is invalid exactly when p1_i+p2_i>T, while LOAD c is invalid exactly when the corresponding total length exceeds T.

The statement's intrinsic dichotomy: JOB is impossible exactly when p1_i + p2_i > T, while LOAD is the one-dimensional pairwise-separation packing condition whose obstruction is the total size exceeding T, together with the promise that one of these certificates exists.

The separation/boundary and bounded-dispersion subsystems admit an exact additive threshold characterization: JOB i is invalid iff q1,i + q2,i > T, and LOAD c is invalid iff the sum of all q_{c,i} exceeds T.
